questions.prompt: You're registering a service in ASP.NET Core that takes a DbContext in its constructor. Which lifetime?
options: Transient, with a static cache inside
It doesn't matter — the container sorts it out
questions.explanation: DbContext isn't thread-safe and it tracks changes for one unit of work, which in a web app means one request. Scoped gives you exactly that. Register it as a singleton and you get entity tracking bleeding between users' requests — a bug that only shows up under real traffic.

questions.prompt: Someone calls an async method with .Result to keep a method signature synchronous. What's the actual risk?
options: Nothing — it's the same thing with extra steps.
Thread-pool starvation and deadlocks once the endpoint is under load.
It adds a fixed ~200ms to every call.
questions.explanation: Blocking on .Result holds a thread hostage while it waits. One or two are invisible; a few hundred concurrent requests and the pool has nothing left to schedule with. The exception answer is half true — they get wrapped in an AggregateException, not swallowed — which is exactly why it's a tempting wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Your Web API returns 200 with an empty body when the posted model is invalid, instead of a 400 with the validation errors. What's most likely missing?
options: A try/catch around the action body
questions.explanation: [ApiController] is what wires up automatic model-state validation and the ProblemDetails 400 response. Without it, ModelState is populated but nobody checks it, so the action runs on garbage input and returns whatever it returns.

questions.prompt: This ASP.NET Core action works locally but degrades badly under load. What is the central problem?
options: Blocking on asynchronous I/O ties up request threads and can cause thread-pool starvation; make the action async and await the call.
HttpClient cannot be used in a controller.
The method needs the static keyword.
questions.explanation: Sync-over-async blocks a worker while the network is idle. Under concurrency those blocked workers accumulate, latency rises, and the pool struggles to serve new requests. Async all the way preserves request capacity.
